newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia to liberalise futures traders licensing.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia to liberalise futures traders licensing.

text.p: Malaysia's Securities Commission (SC) said on Wednesday that it plans to liberalise the licensing scheme governing futures traders.
SC chairman Munir Majid said the dual licensing of representatives at securities dealer firms as representatives of futures brokers will be liberalised through an amendment of existing laws.
Under the liberalisation, a futures and stockbrokers representative licence holder can perform the two functions from the same office.

"The KLSE (Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange) has within its rules a prohibition against dealers' representatives taking on activities not related to stockbroking," Munir said in a speech at a seminar on interest rate futures.
"This effectively prohibits them from selling derivative products which are traded on KLOFFE (Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange)," he said.
He said a futures industry committee would be set up to handle emergencies and situations which could lead to instabilities in the market.
The committee would consist of representatives from KLOFFE, Malaysia Monetary Exchange and the Malaysian Derivatives Clearing House.
Munir said the committee would be set up as soon as necessary amendments to rules governing KLOFFE and MME are made.

Munir said to further improve liquidity on KLOFFE, there was a plan to introduce market-making. "This would not only apply to options contracts, both on the futures as well as on individual stocks, but would have a salutory effect on the liquidity of futures contracts as well," he said.
MME already has 10 market makers, who accounted for 51 percent of total trading in October 1996. MME trades interest rate futures.
However, KLOFFE, which trades stock index futures, was launched in December 1995 without market makers.
Munir said the Malaysian Cabinet had recently decided to merge the Commodities Trading Commission and the Securities Commission.
"With the merger, the regulatory framework for commodity and financial futures will be harmonised," he said.
Munir said the proposed changes were aimed at developing Malaysia's capital markets.
The growth of these markets would help meet "the government's aspiration to promote Kuala Lumpur as a regional financial centre," Munir said.
Malaysia has been liberalising its financial markets and introducing new infrastructure to compete with other regional financial hubs like Hong Kong and Singapore.
